requirement_title: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly
requirement_text:
# REQ-2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129
Type: feature

## Requirement

Given Project A (contains `ProjectA.MyType`, has no and cannot have a reference to the MessagePack NuGet package) and Project B (references Project A and MessagePack), the reporter needs a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for `ProjectA.MyType` generated inside Project B.

Proposed solution: add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that works for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

The class does not need a body; the implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

For attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), the issue lists three alternatives: (1) use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes; (2) let the generator and analyzers work with user-defined copies of the MessagePack attributes; (3) source-generate the attributes themselves via `RegisterPostInitializationOutput`.

Motivation: Project A is a NuGet library that should stay minimal with zero dependencies.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute exists and can be applied to a partial class implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.
- The source generator emits the formatter implementation for `T` inside the annotated class, in the assembly that declares the class (Project B), even when `T` is declared in a referenced assembly.
- The annotated class may be declared without a body (`partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;`).
- `T` needs no MessagePack attributes: without `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` on `T` the generated formatter uses contractless behaviour over public members. (derived from maintainer comment)
- If `T` does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Private members are not required to be serialized; only public members are in scope. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Project A needs no reference to the MessagePack package. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- AArnott: "We might simplistically say this only works in 'contractless' mode, such that you need no attributes on it at all. If there are attributes on it, fine, we'll use them. But if there is no `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` attribute on the type, go contractless by default."
- AArnott on prerequisite: "Does ProjectA.MyType requires only `public` members to be serialized? That seems a prerequisite for anything here." Reporter: yes.
- AArnott is not a fan of a `PropertyKeys` dictionary on the formatter, and warns that copying attributes into Project A breaks reflection-based (dynamic resolver) mode.
- AArnott suggested a surrogate-type design: `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter(SurrogateType = typeof(ProjectASurrogate))]`, keys mapped by property name; reporter: "Looks good." No design was settled in the thread.

product-context: deliberate per ledger, not a defect: Referenced-assembly types are normally skipped by TypeCollector, so no formatter is generated for them. The new GeneratedFormatterCollector deliberately bypasses that skip for types named in [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]. This is an explicit opt-in and consistent with the requirement and the ledger.

product-context: deliberate per ledger, not a defect: The surrogate design plus the contractless default was not settled in the thread, but the ledger answers the intent question: follow the requirement.
Receipts/GeneratedFormatterForReferencedTypeTests.cs: requirement test fails on head: 1/3 failed
Receipts/GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 5/5 failed

Mutation: 11 killed, 5 survived, 3 compile errors, 0 timeouts (19 mutants on MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.cs, GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs, ObjectSerializationInfo.cs, GeneratorUtilities.cs, MessagePackGenerator.cs, MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs)
Compatibility bytes: 4/124 cases differ, 0 base payloads fail to read on head, public API +3/-0

findings.claim: MessagePack attributes on T are ignored. Without a surrogate, the collector always takes the contractless path over every public read-write member. It never reads [MessagePackObject], [Key] or [IgnoreMember] on T, nor [DataContract], [DataMember] or [IgnoreDataMember]. The acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' is therefore not met. For example, a member marked [IgnoreMember] on T is still serialized, and [Key(0)] int keys become string keys.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterForReferencedTypeTests.AttributedReferencedType_IgnoreMemberIsHonoured. T in the referenced assembly has [MessagePackObject], [Key(0)] Id and [IgnoreMember] Secret. The test asserts the generated formatter source never mentions 'Secret'; on head it does.

findings.claim: The change includes an unrelated runtime edit to the timestamp writer. The timestamp32 check now tests the LOW 32 bits of data64 instead of the high 32 bits. Two consequences follow. Ordinary DateTimes with zero nanoseconds now take the 10-byte timestamp64 form instead of the 6-byte timestamp32 form, which is a wire-format change. Values whose low 32 bits are zero but high bits are not (e.g. 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z plus 1 tick) are written as timestamp32 with the truncated value (uint)data64 == 0, so the nanoseconds are silently lost. Nothing in the requirement asks for this.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize new DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc) with base-built and head-built MessagePack: base emits d6 ff + 4 bytes, head emits d7 ff + 8 bytes. Also round-trip new DateTime(1970,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc).AddTicks(1) through MessagePackSerializer on head: the deserialized value loses the tick (data corruption).

findings.claim: The timestamp size check now masks the low 32 bits instead of the high 32 bits, which corrupts data and changes the wire format. If the low 32 bits of `data64` are zero (for example 1970-01-01T00:00:00.0000001Z, or 2106-02-07T06:28:16Z), the 6-byte timestamp32 form is used. It writes `(uint)data64`, which is 0, so the value deserializes as the Unix epoch and the nanoseconds and high seconds are lost. Every ordinary whole-second DateTime that used to encode as 6 bytes now encodes as 10-byte timestamp64.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.TimestampWriterReceipts. EpochPlusOneTickRoundTrips, Year2106BoundaryRoundTrips and WholeSecondUsesTimestamp32 all fail on head because the round trip returns the epoch and the encoding is 10 bytes, not 6.

findings.claim: MessagePack attributes on the formatted type are never honoured. With no SurrogateType, the collector always uses CreateContractlessMembers, which emits string keys over all public read-write members. It ignores [MessagePackObject], [Key(int)] and [IgnoreMember] (and [DataContract]/[DataMember]) declared on T. So a referenced type with `[MessagePackObject]` and `[Key(0)]`/`[Key(1)]`/`[IgnoreMember]` gets a map-mode formatter that also serializes the ignored member. This contradicts the acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured'.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.AttributedReferencedTypeHonoursIntKeys. On head the generated MyTypeFormatter calls WriteMapHeader rather than WriteArrayHeader.

findings.claim: IsPartial checks only the formatter's own declaration. When the formatter is nested in a non-partial containing class, the generated file re-declares the containing type to nest the partial formatter body. The output then fails to compile with CS0260, and no MsgPack019 or other generator diagnostic is reported.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.NestedInNonPartialOuterIsDiagnosedOrCompiles. On head the output compilation contains CS0260 and the generator reports no diagnostic.

findings.claim: The mask in the timestamp writer was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. The timestamp32 branch (6 bytes) is now chosen when the low 32 bits are zero rather than when the high 32 bits are zero. Existing DateTime values will serialize as the wrong format and be corrupted. For example, a time with zero nanoseconds and seconds below 2^32 now falls into the 64-bit timestamp branch. Timestamp32 will be written for values with nonzero nanoseconds, which loses data. This change is unrelated to the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,Utc) and DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,Utc).AddTicks(10) with MessagePackSerializer on base and head builds. Compare the bytes: base emits d6 ff + 4 bytes for the first value, head emits d7 ff + 8 bytes. Round-trip the second value on head to show lost nanoseconds.

findings.claim: Contractless mode skips get-only properties and readonly fields, and sorts members by name. ContractlessStandardResolver serializes get-only members and orders them differently. A user who swaps a formatter from dynamic contractless to the generated one gets different wire bytes, with members missing and key order changed. The ledger says to follow the requirement here, which is ambiguous on this point.

receipt_plan.detail: For a type with public int A {get;set;}, public int B {get;}, and a public field C, serialize with ContractlessStandardResolver and with a generated formatter. Compare the bytes.

findings.claim: An unrelated edit to MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs changes the timestamp encoding check from `0xffffffff00000000` to `0x00000000ffffffff`. This inverts which values use the 6-byte timestamp32 format. It falls outside the feature's scope and affects wire bytes for every user, and numeric serialization is bug-prone per [L16].

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime values with whole seconds (nanoseconds 0) and with nonzero nanoseconds on base and head builds; compare bytes. Base produces timestamp32 (6 bytes) for zero-nanosecond values and head does not.

hunches.claim: The partial formatter body is emitted only in the RegisterSourceOutput(source, ...) path, which is gated on Options.IsGeneratingSource. If that flag requires a [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] declaration, a project that declares only `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;` gets no body and fails with CS0535. That would break the requirement's own minimal example.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterForReferencedTypeTests.FormatterWithoutResolverDeclaration_GeneratesAndCompiles. The test declares only the bodyless formatter for an attribute-free type from a referenced assembly and expects no compile errors.

hunches.claim: The mask in the timestamp writer was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. That inverts the timestamp32 vs timestamp64 selection. Timestamp32 is now chosen when the low 32 bits (seconds) are zero, not when the high 32 bits (nanoseconds and upper seconds) are zero. For a nonzero-seconds, zero-nanosecond DateTime, the encoder now takes the 8-byte timestamp64 path. For a DateTime with seconds==0 but nanoseconds>0, the 6-byte path is taken, which writes only the low 32 bits of data64, so the nanoseconds are silently dropped. The result is corrupted timestamps on serialization, and it is unrelated to this feature.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime values such as 1970-01-01T00:00:00.5Z and 2020-01-01T00:00:00Z with MessagePackWriter.Write(DateTime), then read them back. Round-trip equality fails for the first. Also byte-diff the output between base and head: the format code and length differ (0xd6 vs 0xd7).

hunches.claim: The MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs change flips the timestamp mask from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff, an unrelated runtime change with no covering test. The mutation would select the 6-byte timestamp32 format for wrong values and corrupt DateTime serialization. No test in the diff touches timestamp encoding.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack/MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs:787 swap-boolean/mask: 0x00000000ffffffffL -> 0xffffffff00000000L; expected to survive because no test in the diff serializes timestamps. Also byte-diff: serialize DateTime/DateTimeOffset values (e.g. 2020-01-01 with nanoseconds, and seconds=1) with base and head builds and compare bytes.

hunches.claim: Contractless membership filter IsPublicReadWrite is only tested for a get-only property (Doubled). The tests do not cover public fields, readonly fields, private-setter properties, or inherited members, so mutating the field branch or the base-type walk would survive. Struct tests use properties only.

hunches.claim: Requirement says MessagePack attributes on T must be honoured, but no test puts [MessagePackObject]/[DataContract]/[Key] on T. The collector ignores them entirely. No test would catch this.

receipt_plan.detail: Add a GeneratedMessagePackFormatter over a type annotated with [MessagePackObject] and [Key(n)] on its members (needs MessagePack-referencing type) and assert wire bytes use those keys; it fails on head.

hunches.claim: The surrogate test only covers mixed int-key/ignore handling. There is no execution test for string-key surrogates, or for the key-uniqueness and MemberNeedsKey diagnostics. Mutating `claimedKeys.Add(key)` or the string-key `intKey: members.Count` branch would survive.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs:176 negate-condition: `if (!claimedKeys.Add(key))` -> `if (claimedKeys.Add(key))`; expected to survive because no test has duplicate keys, and the only surrogate has unique int keys (the first mutated run would still emit an error only for distinct keys... tests with unique keys would fail, so also verify with a duplicate-key test).

hunches.claim: The diagnostics tests never assert that generated output is absent or that the non-error cases produce a snapshot. There is no generator snapshot test of emitted code, so the template change (`partial class` vs `internal sealed class`) and the exclusion of attributed classes in GeneratorUtilities are covered only indirectly. Removing the GeneratorUtilities attribute guard would likely survive.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratorUtilities.cs:38 remove-guard: delete `!symbol.GetAttributes().Any(...GeneratedMessagePackFormatter...)`; expected to survive or change only the resolver text because the execution test checks GetFormatter type, which may resolve either way.

hunches.claim: Class without an accessible parameterless constructor, and the inaccessible-type branch of MsgPack021, have no test. Only the abstract case is tested. Also the NoDeserializingConstructor path has none.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs:73 remove-guard: delete the parameterless-constructor check; expected to survive because no test uses a class lacking one.

The analyzer never reports them, because the diagnostics are only reported from the generator. This is an inconsistency, and the new IDs may be missing from AnalyzerReleases.Unshipped.md. interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: As implemented: T is always serialized contractless, over public read-write members with name string keys. Keys and membership can be customised only through a new `SurrogateType` property on [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter], whose [Key]/[IgnoreMember] members are matched by name and type (the maintainer's surrogate suggestion). Attributes on T itself are not read.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: No surrogate. The formatted type's own attributes drive the contract: when T carries [MessagePackObject] or [DataContract], the collector reads [Key]/[IgnoreMember] or [DataMember(Order/Name)]/[IgnoreDataMember] from T's members. This reuses TypeCollector's existing attribute handling (alternative 1 in the issue). It falls back to contractless only when neither attribute is present. Minimal edit: drop SurrogateType, CreateSurrogateMembers and MsgPack022, and branch in Collect on T's attributes before calling CreateContractlessMembers.
